title: the Yoga Vasistha (selections)
hook: a dead king, a grieving queen, and a whole world inside one room
tomorrow: a queen finds peace without leaving home. why does her husband laugh?

segments.voice: Last time, the Yoga Vasistha's four gatekeepers: befriend one, and it brings the others. Now Vasistha starts telling stories, and the first is about grief.

After someone dies, a room can change. A chair, a coat on a hook, a mug nobody else uses. Queen Lila sits in a room like that. King Padma lies dead in the palace, and she can't let him go. Long before, she had prayed to the goddess Sarasvati and been promised that when he died, his spirit wouldn't leave the palace. Now, in her grief, she calls on the goddess again and asks to see where he is. And the goddess shows her.
screen: `A CHAIR, A COAT, A MUG.` → `A QUEEN WHO CAN'T LET GO.` → `WHERE IS HE NOW?`

segments.voice: He's right there, in the space of that very room. But for him, it isn't a room. Inside it, Padma is living another life as a king, with a city, a court and a kingdom around him. Years are passing for him, while for Lila only a short while has gone by. The palace room and the whole kingdom take up the same small space. Vasistha tells Rama this story for the book's big idea. The world that seems so solid, so fixed in size and time, is shaped by the mind. The word he leans on is chitta, the mind, the field where all of it appears. A moment for one person can be years for another. A small room can hold a world. Neither measure is the final one. Think back to Rama at court, sure that nothing was worth holding. Vasistha doesn't argue with him about the world's prizes. He goes underneath them. If the world takes its shape in the mind, then the mind is where the work is done. In this book, yoga isn't mainly about postures. It's the mind seeing how its own worlds are made.
screen: `A KINGDOM INSIDE ONE ROOM.` · `YEARS FOR HIM, MOMENTS FOR HER.` · `CHITTA: WHERE THE WORLD APPEARS.` · then, large: `A SMALL ROOM CAN HOLD A WORLD.`

segments.voice: Choose one small corner of the room you're in: a windowsill, a shelf, the edge of a desk. Look at it for the whole sit as if it held a whole world, and let your eyes find one more detail each time they settle. When the mind wanders off, notice where it went, and come back to the corner.
The Yoga Vasistha: here, Lila's story, a whole kingdom inside one room, because the world takes shape in the mind.
Your line: the Yoga Vasistha, in selections. A small room can hold a world. Day sixteen-oh-four.

sources.ref: Yoga Vasistha, Utpatti Prakarana (the story of Lila: Padma's death, Sarasvati's boon and her showing Lila Padma's new life within the space of the palace room; differing measures of time)

notes: Yoga Vasistha run, day 4. The Lila story is long and layered (Padma's later life as King Viduratha, the earlier Brahmin couple Vasistha and Arundhati); only its first turn is told here. Confirm: Lila's worship of Sarasvati and the boon that the king's spirit would remain in the palace; that Lila asks to see where he has gone; that his new kingdom lies within the space of the room; that much more time passes for him than for her.
For parents: the story opens on a death and a widow's grief; told gently, with no deathbed detail.
The idea 'the world takes shape in the mind' (and the gloss of chitta) is a summary of the book's teaching; a Keeper may prefer different wording or a different Sanskrit term.
Teach's line that the book's yoga 'isn't mainly about postures' is interpretation; confirm. howItsDone's 'best-known' is a superlative about reception; soften if needed.
